items.title: Lessons from Roman concrete

topic.th: วัสดุศาสตร์และวิศวกรรม

paragraphs: Concrete is the most widely used manufactured material on Earth; after water, it is often said to be the substance that people consume in the greatest quantity. Its essential ingredient, cement, is made by heating limestone and clay to around 1,450°C in a kiln, a process that releases carbon dioxide both from the fuel that is burnt and from the limestone itself as it breaks down. Cement manufacture is estimated to account for roughly 8 per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions. Modern reinforced concrete is also surprisingly short-lived: many bridges and buildings from the twentieth century required major repairs within fifty to a hundred years. It is a striking irony, then, that some structures built by the Romans two thousand years ago are still standing, and that a few appear to be stronger now than when they were completed.

Roman builders did not use Portland cement, which was patented in England only in 1824. Instead, they combined lime, produced by heating limestone at lower temperatures than modern kilns reach, with volcanic ash, the finest of which came from deposits around the Bay of Naples. The ash, rich in silica and alumina, reacted with the lime and water to form a binding paste. Writers of the period describe how this mixture was packed down together with chunks of rock or broken brick, rather than poured as a liquid in the way that modern concrete is. The result was denser than might be expected, and its chemistry differed fundamentally from that of the modern material.

The most remarkable examples are the harbour walls and piers that Roman engineers built directly in the sea. For modern concrete, seawater is an enemy: salt penetrates the material and corrodes the steel bars inside, and as the steel rusts and swells, the surrounding concrete cracks. Roman marine concrete contains no steel, and analysis of cores drilled from ancient harbours has revealed something more surprising still. As seawater seeped through the structures over centuries, it dissolved part of the volcanic material and allowed rare minerals to crystallise in the gaps, among them a plate-shaped mineral called aluminous tobermorite. These interlocking crystals appear to have reinforced the material from within, so that contact with the sea, rather than weakening it, gradually made it more cohesive.

A second puzzle concerned the small white lumps of lime scattered through many samples of Roman concrete. Researchers had long dismissed these 'lime clasts' as signs of careless mixing or poor raw materials. More recent studies have proposed another explanation: that the Romans mixed their concrete 'hot', adding quicklime directly instead of first combining it with water. The intense heat of this reaction would have left behind lumps of brittle, calcium-rich material. When a crack later formed and water entered it, the lumps could dissolve and recrystallise as calcium carbonate, sealing the crack. To test the idea, one team made new samples using the hot-mixing method, cracked them deliberately and ran water through them. Within about two weeks the cracks had closed, whereas in otherwise identical samples made without quicklime the water continued to flow.

It would be wrong, however, to conclude that Roman concrete is simply superior. It is considerably weaker in compression than its modern equivalent and takes far longer to reach its full strength, which would be unacceptable on a modern building site, where the timber or metal moulds must be removed and work on the next floor begun within days. Nor could it be used for the slender beams and tall towers of contemporary architecture, which depend on the steel reinforcement that Roman builders did without. Moreover, suitable volcanic ash occurs only in certain regions, and supplying it in the quantities that today's construction industry consumes would be impractical.

What engineers hope to borrow, therefore, is not the Roman recipe but some of its principles. One line of research adds volcanic ash or industrial by-products such as fly ash from power stations to modern mixes, reducing the amount of cement required and, with it, carbon emissions. Another seeks to reproduce the self-healing effect by other means. Some experimental concretes contain dormant bacteria, packed with a food source in tiny capsules; when a crack lets in water, the bacteria become active and produce limestone that fills the gap. Others contain capsules of a liquid healing agent that burst open when the concrete around them cracks.

Whether such materials are adopted widely will depend less on chemistry than on economics and regulation. Self-healing concretes currently cost considerably more than conventional mixes, and building codes, which are based on decades of experience with Portland cement, are slow to accept materials whose long-term behaviour is unknown. Supporters argue that the higher initial price should be weighed against the cost of repairs over a structure's whole life, which can exceed the cost of building it in the first place. If they are right, the most valuable lesson of Roman concrete may be one of perspective: a material should be judged not only by how quickly it can be built with, but by how long it lasts.

items.title: Reading the bones: isotopes and ancient diets

topic.th: โบราณคดี (วิทยาศาสตร์ทางโบราณคดี)

paragraphs: Archaeologists have long tried to reconstruct what people in the past ate, but the traditional evidence is frustratingly partial. Animal bones discarded in rubbish pits show which creatures were butchered, not who ate them; charred seeds survive only if they happened to fall into a fire; and cooking pots preserve traces of little more than the last meals prepared in them. Over the past four decades, a different kind of evidence has transformed the field. Instead of examining the remains of food, researchers now analyse the remains of the eaters themselves, reading in the chemistry of human bone a record of what an individual consumed over many years.

The method rests on the fact that most chemical elements exist in several forms, or isotopes, which differ slightly in mass. Carbon, for example, occurs mainly as carbon-12, with about one per cent as the heavier carbon-13. Plants take up these forms in different proportions as they photosynthesise. Most plants of cooler regions, including wheat, rice and barley, discriminate strongly against the heavier isotope, whereas a group of mainly tropical grasses, among them maize, millet and sugar cane, use a different photosynthetic pathway and retain more of it. Because the saying 'you are what you eat' holds at the molecular level, these differences pass into the tissues of the animals and people who consume the plants, where they can still be detected thousands of years later.

Nitrogen adds a second dimension. Each time nitrogen moves one step up a food chain, from plant to herbivore or from herbivore to carnivore, the proportion of heavy nitrogen-15 increases by a small but fairly predictable amount. A person whose nitrogen values are well above those of the local cattle and sheep therefore probably obtained much of their protein from animals, and especially high values may point to fish from the sea or from lakes, whose food chains are long. Taken together, carbon and nitrogen allow researchers to place individuals on a simple map of diet, distinguishing, say, a farmer who lived largely on cereals from a neighbour who ate a great deal of meat or fish.

Obtaining these numbers is a painstaking process. A small piece of bone, usually from a rib, is first cleaned mechanically to remove soil and any contaminated outer surface. It is then soaked in dilute acid for several days until the mineral component dissolves, leaving behind collagen, the protein that gives bone its flexibility. The collagen is gently heated in weakly acidic water so that it dissolves, filtered to remove remaining impurities and freeze-dried into a fluffy white solid. Less than a milligram of this is then burnt in an instrument called a mass spectrometer, which separates the isotopes by weight and measures their ratio. Before any result is accepted, the laboratory checks the ratio of carbon to nitrogen in the sample, since values outside a narrow range suggest that the collagen has degraded or been contaminated.

Which part of the skeleton is sampled matters a great deal. Bone is living tissue that is constantly broken down and rebuilt, so the collagen in an adult's rib reflects an average of the diet over perhaps the last ten years of life. Teeth behave differently. The dentine inside a tooth forms in layers during childhood and is not afterwards replaced, so thin slices cut along a tooth can reveal how a child's diet changed from year to year, for example the gradual fall in nitrogen values as an infant stopped being breastfed. Comparing the two tissues from the same skeleton can show whether a person ate differently as a child and as an adult, a contrast that has sometimes been read as evidence of migration or of a change in social position.

The technique is not without pitfalls. Collagen survives poorly in hot, wet environments, so the method has worked far better in northern Europe than in much of tropical Asia or Africa, and comparisons between regions are correspondingly lopsided. More fundamentally, isotope values do not identify particular foods. The same reading might result from a diet of millet with a little meat or from rice with plenty of freshwater fish, and other evidence is needed to decide between them. Nor can values be interpreted in isolation, because the isotopic make-up of plants varies with rainfall, soil and even the density of the forest canopy. For this reason, each study must measure the bones of local animals to establish a baseline against which humans can be compared.

Specialists continue to disagree, sometimes sharply, about what the results mean. Dr Ana Ribeiro, who has studied cemeteries in coastal Iberia, argues that differences between men and women in the same community are more common than once supposed, and that they usually reflect unequal access to meat rather than different tastes. Professor Kenji Watanabe has cautioned that many studies rely on too few animal bones, so that apparent contrasts between sites may simply be artefacts of the local environment. Dr Helen Okafor contends that some early farming communities continued to depend heavily on wild foods for centuries, which sits uneasily with the idea of a sudden agricultural revolution. Dr Tomas Lind sees the greatest promise in tooth sections, which he believes offer a rare window on children, who are often invisible in the archaeological record. Dr Priya Nair, finally, insists that isotope results should never stand alone but be read alongside plant remains and residues from pots.

items.title: What should restorers restore?

topic.en: Art history and cultural heritage (conservation ethics)
topic.th: ประวัติศาสตร์ศิลปะและมรดกวัฒนธรรม (จริยธรรมการอนุรักษ์)

paragraphs: In the popular imagination, the restorer of paintings is a kind of rescuer, removing centuries of grime to reveal a work as its maker intended it to be seen. Exhibitions of newly cleaned masterpieces attract large crowds, and the before-and-after photographs that accompany them suggest a simple story of loss followed by recovery. Restorers themselves are seldom so confident, but the language of museums and the press frequently is. I want to suggest that this story, however appealing, misrepresents both what restoration can achieve and what it ought to attempt. The question is not whether old works of art should be cared for, since plainly they should, but whether 'returning a work to its original state' is a coherent goal at all.

Consider first the practical difficulty. Paintings begin to change chemically from the moment they are finished. Some pigments fade in the light while others darken; varnishes turn yellow; canvas and wooden panels expand and contract with changes in humidity, producing networks of fine cracks. Removing a discoloured varnish can certainly bring back brighter colours, but it cannot restore pigments that have themselves altered, and the colours that emerge may therefore be out of balance with one another in a way that the artist never saw. A cleaned painting is not the original painting rediscovered; it is a new state of the object, produced by a modern intervention.

Advocates of thorough cleaning sometimes reply that, whatever its imperfections, a cleaned work is at least closer to the original than a dirty one. This assumes that we know what the original looked like, and often we do not. Documents describing an artist's intentions are rare, and those that survive are open to interpretation. Some painters are known to have applied thin, tinted glazes over the finished surface to soften or unify it, and there is evidence that some of these layers were taken off in past cleanings along with the varnish, because restorers could not distinguish them from later dirt. The confidence with which earlier generations removed such layers should give their successors pause.

There is also the matter of what a work has become over time. An altarpiece that was cut into pieces and sold to different collectors, or a marble statue that lost its painted colours centuries ago, has acquired a history that is now part of what it is. The same is true of buildings: a cathedral altered over five centuries has no single original state to which it could be returned. To 'restore' such an object to an imagined first state is to erase the evidence of that history in favour of a reconstruction that may be largely guesswork. I am not arguing that every effect of time should be preserved untouched; a layer of soot from the candles of a church has little claim to our respect. But the decision about which changes count as damage and which as history is a judgement, not a technical finding, and it should be made openly.

For these reasons, I believe that the guiding principles adopted by most professional conservators over the past half-century are broadly correct. They emerged partly in reaction to the practices of the nineteenth century, when restorers routinely repainted damaged areas in their own style, supplied missing limbs to ancient statues and occasionally 'improved' compositions that they found awkward. Interventions should be the minimum necessary to stabilise a work; any additions should be distinguishable from the original material on close inspection; and, as far as possible, treatments should be reversible, so that a future generation with better knowledge can undo them. These principles reflect a proper humility about the limits of present understanding.

Yet the principles are not as straightforward as they sound. Few treatments are fully reversible in practice: a solvent that removes varnish cannot put it back, and even modern synthetic materials, chosen precisely because they can be dissolved later, may leave traces in the paint. 'Minimum intervention' is also open to dispute, since leaving a damaged area untreated may allow decay to spread. The principles are better understood as aspirations that guide judgement than as rules that settle it, and it is a mistake to present them to the public as guarantees.

Some critics of restoration go further, arguing that works should be left entirely alone except to halt active deterioration. I do not share this view. A painting so obscured by darkened varnish that its subject can barely be made out is not being respected by our inaction; it is simply being lost in a different way. It is worth remembering, too, that such varnish was often applied long after the artist's death and has no special claim to authenticity of its own. Museums exist partly so that people can see works of art, and there are cases in which careful cleaning genuinely serves that purpose. My objection is not to cleaning as such but to cleaning undertaken in the belief that it recovers a single, authentic original.

What, then, should change? Above all, I would like museums to explain their decisions more candidly. Labels and exhibitions could describe not only what was done to a work but also what remained uncertain, which alternatives were considered and what was deliberately left untouched. A few institutions have begun to do this, displaying images made with X-rays or ultraviolet light beside the works themselves. Visitors are perfectly capable of understanding that a painting is a physical object with a history, and many may find that history at least as interesting as the myth of a perfect original. Restoration presented in this way would become not a promise of recovery but an invitation to look more closely.

The table below gives information about the use of public libraries in one country in 2005, 2015 and 2025.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

Write at least 150 words.

Some people argue that governments should fund scientific research only when it is likely to produce practical benefits, such as new medicines or technologies. Others believe that research driven purely by curiosity deserves equal public support, even if it has no obvious use.

Discuss both these views and give your own opinion.

Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Write at least 250 words.
